#1201. Legendary commentator MARTIN TYLER on taking the Premier League plunge in 1992, Arsene Wenger's fury, his love of Woking - and THAT Sergio Aguero moment

Published: 13:55 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 15:04 EST, 18 November 2026

Two football images adorn the walls of Martin Tyler’s new home or at least they will when everything is in order.

Tyler has recently moved house and the large, framed photograph of Teddy Sheringham scoring for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool, the only goal of the first Premier League game broadcast live by Sky is still on the floor by the front door.

From wherever it ends up, it will project a moment in time when everything changed for Tyler, having walked away from a steady job at ITV and taken a leap of faith as lead commentator for the new satellite channel.

'A new frontier,' admits Tyler, the undisputed ‘Voice of the Premier League’ by the time he left the role at Sky, more than 30 years later.

'We didn’t know where it would take us, so that was a special day. Feeling a bit like a pioneer. Wondering whether we were all on a fool’s errand. Some people turned down the job I accepted because of the risk. My kids were four and two at the time.

'We used to travel to the games by train in those days, and we would look out of the window and count the satellite dishes as we passed through a big town. We didn’t know whether it was going to work. I wasn’t sure anybody would be watching.

Legendary football commentator Martin Tyler has released a book: TALES FROM THE GANTRY

Tyler was the undoubted 'Voice of the Premier League' by the time he left Sky Sports in 2023

'It was slow off the ground and there was a feeling within the game against live football, that people wouldn’t go to the games if they were televised live, and it ended up the opposite. Attendances have gone up, an amazing paradox. Now you can’t get a ticket.'

Televised football has come a long way since Tyler’s first commentary game, Southampton v Sheffield Wednesday in the old Division Two in 1974, shot with just four cameras for Southern Television.

'Now if you don’t have 24 cameras you can feel a bit short-changed,' he laughs. 'I worked at ITV for about 17 years, most of it commentating and you would get a crew on match day who had been doing Coronation Street or Emmerdale Farm in the week and a match director from light entertainment.'

The Premier League has come a long way, too. Some might argue too far. It has led football from its roots as the working man’s game to a place where clubs are owned by nations states and mired in the legal complications of the Manchester City case.

Tyler wants to reserve comment on City’s financial offences until sentencing is passed, aware he is inextricably bound to their success because of his iconic commentary for Sergio Aguero’s winner in the 93rd minute against Queen’s Park Rangers to snatch the Premier League title from Manchester United in 2012.

'I’ve always said you won’t see anything like it again, and I stick to that,' he says, although he the 'Aguero moment’ as it has become commonly known probably means less to him than it does to others.

He is proud to deliver the words but insists those moments belong to the players, the clubs and the fans, not to him.

Ask about his favourite game from three decades in the Premier League and Tyler instinctively pulls Liverpool’s 4-3 comeback win against Newcastle in 1996 from the thrillers he has called.

His own footballing background, meanwhile, could hardly be any further from the Premier League’s glitzy, moneyed elite.

Tyler has always supported Woking and played as an amateur for Corinthian-Casuals. 'The law was you couldn’t get paid,' he says. 'We were on expenses only and they weren’t dodgy expenses. If I went on the tube to Leytonstone, I got the tube fare repaid and no more.

'I played for five years at that level and never got a penny because that was the rule. I played my last game in 1973 and within two years’ they got rid of it because so many people were bending the rules. An opposition player told me their team were on £75 a game.'

Tyler reflected on his time in the game as a player, coach and commentator with Daily Mail Sport's Matt Barlow

He was famously on commentary for Sergio Aguero's title-winning moment in 2012

From a cricketing family, Tyler was on the books at Surrey where he twice served as 12th man and lived for a time with Bob Willis, who became one of England’s greatest fast bowlers after moving on to Warwickshire.

His manager for a time at Casuals was Surrey legend Micky Stewart, who had also played for the famous amateur football club before turning professional at Charlton. In those days it was possible for the multi-talented to hold down a decent career in two sports.

An afternoon in Tyler’s company is just as likely to involve digressions into non-league football, where he worked as an assistant to Alan Dowson at clubs including Woking and Hampton & Richmond, as it is into the Premier League.

He might regale you with a story about Arsene Wenger and the time, on the way to the gantry at Wigan Athletic, he slipped deeper than he realised into long conversation with the then Arsenal boss about rioting in Paris and almost missed his pre-match slot.

And he might pivot from there into Wenger’s fierce rivalry with Sir Alex Ferguson. 'I have seen Arsene very, very grumpy,' says Tyler. 'When he lost the FA Cup semi-final when Dennis Bergkamp missed the penalty and Ryan Giggs scored.

'I have never seen a manager so angry because he knew he had handed over not only an FA Cup final place but also the domination they enjoyed at that time. They had done the Double in 98 and he felt that was not only about losing a match but losing their psychological edge over their greatest rivals. He was livid. Talk about winning and losing with dignity.'

But there’s every chance he will reminisce about the time when, as a schoolboy Woking supporter in the terrible winter of 1962-63 he was rewarded for volunteering to paint the stands with an invitation to travel on the team bus to an Amateur Cup tie at Lydbrook Athletic.

'We left Woking at seven on the morning of the match for a two o’clock kick-off in Gloucestershire and by nine we were digging the bus out of a snowdrift on the A4,' says Tyler. 'We got there at four, no floodlights, and they had marked the lines on the snow with blue soap powder but there was no way we could play. We turned around to go back, got stuck in Cheltenham and had to stay for the night.'

The only other footballing image on display in Tyler’s home is a photograph of him and Dowson celebrating as the final whistle confirmed their Hampton & Richmond side as Isthmian League champions in 2016.

Tyler has had a hugely varied career, all the way from grassroots level right to the top

Tyler even worked as an assistant coach to Alan Dowson at several Non-League clubs

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE

After collecting the trophy, Tyler jumped into his car, drove north and less than 24 hours later was at the King Power Stadium to see Leicester crowned champions of England.

'The greatest fairytale story in the Premier League,' as he says. 'I had sampled that in a tiny non-league way, then taken those feelings with me to Leicester where it was multiplied a million times, but I could tell the world a tiny bit about how wonderful they must be feeling.'

The range of his experience is vast. From amateur football in the 60s, through regional television and ITV to Sky’s Premier League revolution. He commentates regularly and coaches at Woking’s academy and has written a book.

It is a wonderful compilation of 110 essays, the reflections on his lifetime in football. 'The random thoughts of a football obsessive,' as he likes to call it.

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE

#1200. Can Mauricio Pochettino replicate hallmark intensity he brought to USMNT with Manchester United?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

From the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system. Indeed, there is such potential for misdiagnosis when assessing running statistics that senior figures at more than one of the best recruiting clubs in England consider their worth to be, at best, dubious.

Too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better. You know who didn't have to peg it all that often? Sergio Busquets, perhaps the best defensive midfielder of his generation, plying his trade for the majority of his career at Barcelona. Keep the ball, read the game, control the territory and you will very quickly find the other team covering plenty more kilometers than you.

Manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season. If there were any correlation between distance covered and results, then the relegation race would be even more exciting than it is shaping up to be, given that Liverpool sit below United on that measure and Manchester City above them. It is quite hard to believe that United are winning fewer games compared to last year (when they had nearly 10% less possession it should be noted) because each player is covering about 45 meters fewer per game. Physical data might not be linked to team quality, then, but it might tell us something relevant if, for instance, United were to hire a coach who prizes dynamic players and demands an intense press at the very top of the pitch. A Mauricio Pochettino type, if you will. The soon-to-be former United States men's national team head coach, handed the task of extricating Manchester United from the relegation zone before molding a contender, is defined by the aggression and energy of his charges. It is why he was the perfect match for a young Tottenham side with a point to prove. It is why Paris Saint-Germain and the Neymar-Kylian Mbappe axis was such an obviously awkward fit from the off.

It is also a template that has worked even when there was cause for skepticism. You couldn't have players sprinting their way across SoFi after the rigors of a club season, said those who doubted the USMNT. He didn't ask much of his team, just "to use your brain while physically, you were killing yourself," as Tim Ream, then 38, said in the summer.

Tell you what, though, it worked. The United States' World Cup campaign might have ended at about the time and in the fashion that most expected, but at their best, they were pressing dynamos. Their 10.16 passes allowed per defensive action (PPDA) -- a measure of press intensity -- placed them sixth among the 48 teams at the World Cup, rubbing shoulders with the likes of Germany, Spain and Uruguay, coached by Pochettino's mentor and high priest of the high press Marcelo Bielsa. No team that reached the knockouts forced their opponents to misplace a higher proportion of their passes than the U.S., 22.8%.

Pochettino might have framed much of his work around changing the culture of the USMNT, but that was a job that was easier to do with a player pool that suited his needs. His squad was strong, organized and, most importantly of all, athletic.

That is not a term that is particularly associated with Manchester United. Indeed, according to Gradient Sports, one of the leading external providers of physical data in football, Pochettino's new team is the least athletic in the Premier League. Based on Gradient's athleticism score -- which combines a host of physical data points including accelerations and decelerations, sprint distance and max speed -- United and Nottingham Forest are cut adrift from the rest of the league. In average max speed of outfield players, United also rank 19th out of 20, 5% slower than the fleet-footed Bournemouth and Liverpool.

The months to come may prove that United look unathletic because that's how Michael Carrick wanted them to play, controlling possession and building more steadily than the sides who rushed headfirst into any counter that came their way. Instinctively, though, that does not feel like the United of Harry Maguire, Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo, does it?

The three center backs who have started the bulk of United's Premier League games this season -- Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven -- all rank around the bottom third or lower of players in their position in terms of top speed, accelerations and decelerations and percentage of runs at high speeds (20-25 km/h), according to Gradient data. It is a similar story for the midfielders, particularly Andrey Santos, Mainoo and Tielemans. The one central midfield option with an impressive athletic profile, Carlos Baleba, is out injured. It seemed bitterly ironic that Baleba's hamstring went after a driving run through midfield. The sheer act of high-intensity running does sometimes look like it puts an unbearable strain on United legs.

That might be why they do it so little. Opta judges that Santos applies pressure to 56.2% of his opponents' touches, Tielemans 56.8%, Bruno Fernandes 57% and Mainoo 57.3%. All of them sit in the bottom 12 in the league among midfielders with 300 or more minutes. Marcus Rashford, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Amad Diallo occupy spots one, three, five and six in terms of the top flight's least pressing-y forwards.

Now, of course, Pochettino can adapt. After all, he has just implemented a surprisingly effective high press in a side captained by Ream (sorry, Tim!). A lot of the Chelsea squad he took over in 2023-24 did not look to be at ease hunting the ball, but he still had them above league average in PPDA, opponent pass completion, ball recoveries and in particular duel success in the final third. A bit more oomph is not beyond these United players, as they showed last season.

However, it is particularly curious to finally alight on Pochettino, whom they could have hired at least half a dozen times in the past, when the squad seems so ill-suited to his principles. We might not be able to tell from physical data whether this team was giving its all for Carrick -- and, by extension, whether there is another gear for the new manager to drive them to -- but what we can see is certainly enough to raise the question of why the powers that be at United think that this is a squad ready to play Pochettino-style.

“On every level, he has delivered: points per game, net spend, a distinguishable style of play, improving individual players, over-performance in the league and European competition.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

#1197. Mykhailo Mudryk reveals he spent 'MILLIONS' on legal bills to fight doping charge as he blames his stint with Ukraine for two-year ban in tell-all interview

Published: 19:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 18 November 2026

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed his stint with the Ukrainian national team for the failed doping test which cost him two years of his career and revealed how fighting his case personally cost him millions of pounds.

The Chelsea winger, who is now on loan with Tottenham Hotspur, has opened up for the first time since he returned to football in the summer when his suspension was suddenly lifted.

It was in a two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel. While the title of the video mentions ‘suicidal thoughts’, Mudryk clarifies during the conversation that he did not consider committing suicide despite being in a dark place. ‘Kill myself – no, that’s not a way out,’ he said when asked that question.

But he did discuss how Chelsea broke the news of his failed test to him, whether they helped their £89million signing from Shakhtar Donetsk during his ban, his belief that the drug meldonium entered his system while he was in Ukraine, and why he is now with Tottenham. He further claimed that he has faced threats from gangsters, and admitted his dream is to someday win the Ballon d’Or.

On the Ukrainian national team and their federation, the Ukrainian Association of Football, Mudryk said: ‘I’ll be honest, it pretended to help. But in reality, there was no help. They created more problems than they solved. Especially when we needed help the most, they turned their backs on us.

'I just would like, for the future, everyone to understand that you can only rely on yourself.'

Mykhailo Mudryk has spoken publicly for the first time about the doping case that cost him two years of his career

Mudryk has criticised the Ukrainian Association of Football over their support during his case

Daily Mail Sport contacted the Ukrainian Association of Football for comment.

Continuing, Mudryk said: ‘The UAF is afraid of being left to blame in this situation, and afraid of the criticism or whatever else might come raining down. Distancing themselves from their own player, not helping, pretending to help, and in the end, first they drag the case out for months without really helping the case in the end. But at least the UAF isn’t to blame.’

Mudryk was handed an initial four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test, with his last appearance prior to that coming in November 2024 in the Conference League away at Heidenheim. He scored in that 2-0 win for Chelsea. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'. Mudryk appeared for Chelsea during their pre-season tour before joining Tottenham on loan.

On how and why he failed his test, Mudryk said: ‘I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It’s a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe.

‘This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that’s Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

‘I was at home and Chelsea’s management came to see me and they said we needed to talk. Then they say you’ve returned a positive doping test and now you’re facing a ban.

‘You can’t believe it’s true. You can’t believe this is happening to you. If I’d ever taken anything anywhere, I’d have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

‘At least I’d have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that’s the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

‘Otherwise there’d be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don’t hear them.

Mudryk returned to action when his ban was lifted in August, with the winger revealing Xabi Alonso told him to get game time and that he was 'counting on him'

The Ukrainian joined Tottenham on loan but has seen injury restrict his involvement to date

‘At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you’re falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You’re flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don’t wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.’

Mudryk revealed how ‘the figure is in the millions’ when asked about the lawyers fees which were needed to fight his case. He confirmed he paid for that himself, along with the personal trainers and massage therapists he used to maintain his fitness while suspended. However, Mudryk did add that Chelsea continued to pay his salary during his time out of football.

On joining Tottenham and being reunited with Roberto De Zerbi, who formerly managed him at Shakhtar Donetsk, Mudryk said: ‘It’s a perfectly logical decision. The club (Chelsea) has a new coach (Xabi Alonso), he sees football his own way. He sees the players he needs for that football. He came up and told me straight to my face: “You’d better go and play, get some game time, and then come back to Chelsea. I’m counting on you.”’ On De Zerbi, he added: ‘We met and he says: “Are you happy? Come on, we’ve still got a lot of work to do together.”’

Mudryk added how difficult it was after switching to England and, along with encountering issues with his former representatives who encouraged him to move to Chelsea rather than Arsenal, he said: 'They give you ultimatums, you know. That’s how it is.’

#1196. Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2. Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented2, the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2. However, its occurrence is highly context-dependent, and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In humans, cannibalism largely disappeared with cultural evolution, partly owing to prion diseases3. Similarly, insects such as crickets rarely engage in cannibalism under normal conditions, but confinement or nutritional deprivation can trigger this behaviour4. These observations highlight the influence of environmental pressures on cannibalism, although its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms remain unclear.

Locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its important role in collective dynamics5,6. In juvenile migratory bands, the threat of conspecific predation from behind promotes forward movement, reducing cannibalistic risk and contributing to group cohesion5,6. Cannibalism also provides nutritional benefits, allowing locusts to compensate for food deficiencies and potentially enhancing survival and movement capacity7,8. This behaviour is strongly influenced by density-dependent phase polyphenism. At low densities, solitarious locusts avoid conspecifics, whereas increased population density promotes gregarious behaviour and cannibalistic encounters5,7. Nutritional deficiencies further exacerbate cannibalism. Field studies of South American locusts (Schistocerca cancellata) have demonstrated that carbohydrate deprivation promotes cannibalism9, whereas laboratory studies on desert locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) have shown that protein-biased diets reduce movement and increase cannibalistic interactions7. Although these findings establish the ecological importance of cannibalism, its molecular and genetic regulation remains poorly understood.

Chemical cues regulate diverse locust behaviours, including aggregation10,11, oviposition12, mating13 and cannibalism14. Our previous work identified phenylacetonitrile (PAN) as a density-dependent anticannibalistic pheromone that activates specific olfactory receptors and reduces conspecific predation in crowded populations14. However, whether chemical cues actively induce cannibalism has remained unclear. Field and laboratory observations indicate that injured locusts are preferentially targeted by conspecifics15, suggesting that injury-induced chemical signals may attract individuals and promote cannibalistic behaviour.

Guaiacol, a volatile compound produced by gut microbiota during plant digestion, has been identified as an aggregation pheromone in desert locusts16. Here we show that injury-induced microbiota-derived guaiacol coordinates immune defence and cannibalism in migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms, which span microbial biosynthesis, olfactory detection, immune regulation and behavioural responses. Together, our findings identify a microbial signalling mechanism linking immunity and cannibalism, revealing how host–microbe interactions mediate a trade-off between immune protection and vulnerability to conspecific predation.

Cannibalism in L. migratoria exhibits phase polyphenism, with solitarious nymphs typically avoiding conspecific predation, whereas gregarious nymphs are more prone to engage in cannibalism, particularly under conditions of crowding or food scarcity14. Preliminary observations indicated that injured individuals were rapidly surrounded and attacked by nearby conspecifics (Fig. 1a), suggesting that injury itself serves as a cue that increases susceptibility to conspecific predation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dual-choice assays with gregarious fourth- and fifth-instar nymphs, the developmental stages at which cannibalism is most prevalent14. As injury can alter locomotor performance and therefore influence predator choice independently of injury-derived signals, we controlled for this potentially confounding factor by immobilizing both prey individuals. This experimental design enabled us to specifically evaluate the contribution of injury-associated cues to predator preference. In each assay, pairs of immobilized intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs were presented at opposite ends of a chamber containing ten starved fifth-instar predators (Fig. 1b). Injuries were induced either mechanically or by previous conspecific bites. Across all assays, predators consistently exhibited a marked predation preference for injured over intact prey, indicating a significant role of injury in heightening vulnerability to conspecific predation (Fig. 1c).

Ten starved fifth-instar gregarious nymphs were presented with one intact and one injured fourth-instar nymph immobilized at opposite ends of the arena. c–f, Predation preferences of intact (c; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.009; group 2, P = 0.012), ommatidectomized (d; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.001; group 2, P = 0.006), antennectomized (e; n = 15) and LmOrco−/− (f; n = 14) nymphs. Three prey pairings were tested: group 1, intact versus bitten; group 2, intact versus mechanically injured; group 3, mechanically injured versus bitten. g, Schematic of the dual-choice olfactometer assay testing volatiles from intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs. h,i, Olfactory preference of wild-type (h; n = 19; group 1, P = 0.010; group 2, P < 0.001) and LmOrco−/− (i; n = 15) nymphs for the three pairings described above. In c–f, preference is expressed as the percentage of total prey body mass consumed from each prey individual. All behavioural data are presented as box-and-whisker plots (boxes represent median and upper/lower quartiles; centre lines indicate the median, plus signs indicate the mean and whiskers extend from the minimum to the maximum values). Statistical analyses were performed using two-sided paired-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. ***P < 0.001; ** P < 0.01; * P < 0.05; NS, not significant.

To determine whether the type of injury influenced predation preference, we compared predator preferences between mechanically injured and bitten prey. No significant difference was observed (Fig. 1c), indicating that injury alone, regardless of its origin, is sufficient to induce preferential predation. To explore whether injury-induced vulnerability was consistent across developmental stages, we extended the assays to first- to fifth-instar nymphs as prey. In all stages tested, fifth-instar predators consistently preferred injured prey over their intact counterparts, irrespective of injury type (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These findings demonstrate that injury-driven cannibalism is a robust and consistent trait across the development of gregarious locusts.

Next, we investigated the sensory cues mediating injury-induced predation. To assess the roles of olfactory and visual inputs, we performed antennal ablation (disrupting primary olfactory input), knocked out olfactory coreceptor LmOrco (disrupting olfactory receptor function) (Extended Data Fig. 1b) or removed the compound eyes (disrupting visual input). Predators with removed compound eyes retained their preference for injured prey (Fig. 1d), suggesting that visual cues are not required to mediate this behaviour. By contrast, predators lacking antennae or LmOrco function showed no preference for injured over intact prey (Fig. 1e,f). Notably, although antennectomized predators no longer exhibited a statistically significant preference, a weak residual bias towards injured prey remained (Fig. 1e). This observation was consistent with the anatomical organization of the locust olfactory system, in which the antennae constitute the principal but not the exclusive olfactory organs. Consequently, antennal removal might substantially reduce but not completely eliminate olfactory perception. By contrast, disruption of LmOrco, which broadly impairs odorant receptor function, resulted in a complete loss of discriminatory behaviour (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings identify LmOrco-dependent olfaction as the primary sensory modality mediating injury-induced cannibalistic predation.

Finally, we assessed whether volatile chemical cues contributed to the observed predation bias. Headspace volatiles from both injured and intact nymphs were collected and presented in a dual-choice olfactometer (Fig. 1g). Starved fifth-instar predators strongly preferred the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals over the zone containing volatiles from intact prey (Fig. 1h). No significant difference in preference was observed between volatiles from mechanically versus bitten prey (Fig. 1h), indicating that injury-induced volatile release enhances predator attraction, thereby increasing the susceptibility of injured individuals to cannibalism. By contrast, LmOrco−/− predators showed no preference for the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals (Fig. 1i), indicating that LmOrco-dependent olfaction mediated the predation preference.

To investigate the chemical signals underlying injury-induced cannibalism in L. migratoria, we analysed the headspace volatiles emitted by intact, mechanically injured and bitten locust nymphs (Fig. 2a). Among the compounds detected, guaiacol emerged as the dominant injury-affected odorant (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Table 1), with emission levels approximately ten-fold higher in injured nymphs compared with intact controls and gregarious adults (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This increase in guaiacol release was consistent across all developmental instars (first to fifth) (Extended Data Fig. 2c), suggesting that an increase in guaiacol production is a consistent physiological response to injury in gregarious nymphs. By contrast, other compounds—including PAN, which has previously been linked to suppression of cannibalism14—showed no significant changes across injury conditions (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating that guaiacol is a key injury cue.

To assess the behavioural significance of guaiacol, we conducted dual-choice olfactometer assays with fifth-instar nymphs and male and female adults from both gregarious and solitarious phases, testing the effects of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Table 2) at a concentration of 10−3 (Fig. 2d). Only gregarious nymphs exhibited strong attraction to guaiacol; solitarious individuals and gregarious adults showed no significant preference (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Video 1). This indicated that guaiacol selectively attracts gregarious nymphs. We then investigated whether the naturally emitted levels of guaiacol from injured gregarious nymphs were sufficient to trigger attraction. Quantitative headspace analysis showed that emissions from injured gregarious nymphs corresponded to concentrations equivalent to 10−5 to 10−4 dilutions of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2e). To determine whether these natural guaiacol emissions were sufficient to induce attraction, we tested behavioural responses of gregarious nymphs using a full concentration series (10−7 to 10−2) in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 2d). Attraction to guaiacol emerged sharply at 10−6 and remained robust at higher concentrations but disappeared at 10−7 (Fig. 2f). This aligned with the physiological range of natural emissions from injured nymphs, confirming that guaiacol concentrations released by injured individuals are behaviourally relevant. As all preceding behavioural assays were conducted with individually tested locusts, we next examined whether guaiacol attraction was preserved under the social conditions that characterize gregarious populations. To address this question, we performed dual-choice olfactometer assays using groups of five gregarious nymphs and quantified the average time spent by the group on each side of the arena. Consistent with the results obtained from individually tested animals, groups of gregarious nymphs spent significantly more time on the side containing 10−3 guaiacol than on the control side (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Video 2). These findings demonstrate that the attractive effect of guaiacol persists in a group context and therefore probably operates under ecologically relevant social conditions.

As attraction alone does not necessarily imply a decision to engage in cannibalistic behaviour, we next investigated whether guaiacol could directly trigger cannibalistic predation. We performed two-choice predation assays, providing pairs of intact fourth-instar gregarious nymphs—one treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol (representing natural emission levels from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) and the other with solvent oil—to 10 starved fifth-instar gregarious predators (Fig. 2g). Guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially consumed, whereas solvent-treated nymphs were rarely attacked (Fig. 2h), confirming that guaiacol is a potent elicitor of cannibalistic predation. We then sought to rule out the potential influence of endogenous guaiacol on predator preference. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol is primarily synthesized by gut microbiota during plant digestion in locusts16. To eliminate this confounding factor, we generated germ-depleted gregarious nymphs by administering a cocktail of three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin) in their feed17,18,19 (Fig. 2i). This approach effectively abolished guaiacol emission in both intact and injured nymphs, providing a chemically clean background for subsequent behavioural assays (Fig. 2j). We then treated the germ-depleted gregarious nymphs with 2 µl of either 10−4 guaiacol (mimicking natural release from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) or solvent oil and used them as prey in dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 2i). As observed previously, guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially attacked, and solvent-treated nymphs were largely ignored (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Finally, to evaluate the ecological relevance of guaiacol-mediated cannibalism under more naturalistic conditions, we performed semi-field experiments in large outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 500 fifth-instar gregarious predators, together with 100 fourth-instar prey perfumed with either 10−4 guaiacol or solvent alone (Extended Data Fig. 2h). After 24 h, substantially fewer fourth-instar nymphs remained in guaiacol-treated enclosures than in control enclosures, indicating a significantly higher frequency of cannibalistic interactions in the presence of guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Consistent with direct behavioural observations, the reduction in surviving individuals was attributable to increased conspecific predation rather than escape, as all locusts were confined within the enclosure. These findings demonstrate that guaiacol-mediated promotion of cannibalism persists at the population level under seminatural conditions, supporting the ecological relevance of this injury-associated signal. Collectively, these findings establish guaiacol as a critical chemical cue that both signals injury and induces conspecific predation.

To elucidate the molecular basis of guaiacol detection in L. migratoria, we sought to identify the specific olfactory receptors involved. In our previous study, we identified LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 as receptors responsive to guaiacol, on the basis of functional characterization of 49 L. migratoria olfactory receptors20. To confirm whether other olfactory receptors were involved in detection of this compound, we expanded our analysis to include a panel of 82 of approximately 140 identified L. migratoria olfactory receptors (Fig. 3a). Consistent with our earlier findings, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 exhibited robust responses to guaiacol in a heterologous expression system (Fig. 3a,b), while no other receptor showed comparable sensitivity.
